claims.claim_text: The power MOSFET was developed at International Rectifier in the late 1970s by a very small group; the basic patents were held exclusively and returned close to a billion dollars in royalties before expiring.
claims.quote_verbatim: my first challenge was to build a better transistor. And my friend from graduate school, Tom Herman, and I came up with something that's now called the Power MOSFET
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: Bipolar transistors dominated power work before the MOSFET and had three compounding weaknesses: limited switching speed, a safe operating area problem that made them fragile, and limited gain.
claims.quote_verbatim: also fairly delicate. They had a safe operating area problem. And they also had limited gain
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: The HexFET came from injecting extra charge into a region that was too narrow so that it presented itself as wider to the electrons; the device went from 2 ohms to 0.7 ohms on the second attempt at building it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the idea was to inject extra charge in that too narrow region, which would, in fact, make it look wider to the electrons
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: The IGBT is structurally a FET that trades the low-resistance N-plus substrate for a P substrate, which makes it behave partly like a bipolar and gives lower effective on-resistance specifically at high voltages — which is why high-voltage work moved to IGBTs while CoolMOS answered from the other direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: the third step was in the later 80s was the IGBT. And that is really a variant of a FET in that it trades the low resistance N plus substrate with a P substrate
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: On-resistance for a given die area has fallen from the ohms of the first power MOSFETs to micro-ohms, a span of roughly six orders of magnitude over the device's commercial life.
claims.quote_verbatim: now we're talking micro ohms for the same size die
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: Silicon is cheap partly through tooling but fundamentally because the bond between its atoms is weak, so little energy is needed to form the crystal. Silicon carbide's strong bond is exactly what makes it a wide bandgap material and also what makes it permanently more expensive — no process change can make a silicon carbide crystal as cheap as silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's cheap because the bond between silicon atoms isn't very strong
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: Growing gallium nitride as a micron-thin layer on standard silicon, demonstrated in 1999, is what sidesteps the compound-semiconductor cost problem: you get the wide bandgap without paying to grow the expensive crystal.
claims.quote_verbatim: 1999, Japanese researchers figured out how to grow gallium nitride as a thin layer on top of silicon
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: Gallium nitride wins on three independent counts: higher electron mobility, a wide bandgap that lets high-voltage terminals sit closer together without breaking down so the device can be physically smaller, and a two-dimensional electron gas that runs along the surface and supports very efficient lateral devices — theoretically thousands of times more efficient than a vertical silicon structure.
claims.quote_verbatim: nitride also has higher electron mobility
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: Building a simulation model from a datasheet alone is essentially impossible for a bipolar because the quasi-saturation region is never documented well enough; for a MOSFET it is achievable and good enough for switching power supply work, but only by bringing assumptions the datasheet does not supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: making a model from a data sheet is essentially impossible
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: The workable modelling procedure is to build test fixtures that reproduce the datasheet's own curves — output characteristics, on-resistance against gate voltage, and gate charge — then adjust model parameters until the simulated curves match. Even done expertly it takes around 45 minutes per device.
claims.quote_verbatim: make little test fixtures that will curve trace
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Frequently no physical device matches its own datasheet, because different curves were extracted from different sample transistors: the gate-charge plot may come from a part with a different threshold voltage than the one used for the output characteristics, so no single model can satisfy both.
claims.quote_verbatim: there often is no transistor that behaves like the data sheet. There's no transistor that exists
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Rather than modelling an unmodelled part, sort the simulator's existing device library by gate charge and then by on-resistance, find an entry matching both, and simulate with that — the sourcing decision is then independent of which model you simulated.
claims.quote_verbatim: sorting them first by the gate charge and then by the RDS on and then find a MOSFET with the same RDS on and the same gate charge
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Expecting a model from the manufacturer misreads the skill involved: simulation plays no part in designing a power MOSFET, so the people who build the best devices have no particular reason to be able to model them.
claims.quote_verbatim: is not part of power MOSFET design. There's no reason why somebody who knows how to make the best power MOSFET in the world would know how to make a SPICE model
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: A power MOSFET's channel is roughly half a micron long and on the order of ten metres wide — an older device perhaps five — folded up inside a package small enough to hold, which is what the design goal of as wide and as short as possible produces physically.
claims.quote_verbatim: the practical dimensions of a power MOSFET channel is a half micron long and 10 meters wide
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: A power MOSFET's gate-drain capacitance depends on whether the device is conducting, because the channel lies between gate and drain and its state changes the effective separation. In a lateral integrated MOSFET, where gate and drain sit side by side above the channel, the capacitance barely moves — which is why the two device types need different charge models.
claims.quote_verbatim: in a power transistor, the channel is in between the gate and the drain. So whether it's conducting or not, it moves the distance between the gate and drain
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Gate-drain capacitance is the Miller capacitance and it determines switching behaviour, so a model without a state-dependent charge model does not merely lose accuracy — it does not behave like a power MOSFET at all, which is exactly why simulated waveforms failed to resemble bench measurements until a dedicated model was written.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have a device that behaves like a power MOSFET at all
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: A simulator's default beta parameter for a MOSFET is sized for a small-signal device; at an amp of current through a power device it produces an inexplicable voltage drop across the part until the value is raised to something like eighty or calculated properly.
claims.quote_verbatim: the default value is small, which is for a small signal MOSFET, but for a power MOSFET
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mute Button Discipline

claims.claim_text: Beta is a bipolar parameter meaning current gain and has no standard meaning for a MOSFET, because the bipolar is a current-driven device and the field-effect device is voltage-driven — where a parameter name carries over between the two families it usually means something else.
claims.quote_verbatim: are current driven devices and MOSFETs are voltage driven devices
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mute Button Discipline

claims.claim_text: The Miller plateau — the gate charge levelling off at a particular gate-source voltage rather than continuing to ramp — is mostly a concern in high-current driver and motor work, and gate series resistance is the usual lever for managing what happens through it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Miller plateau is where you charge
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: Devices drawn close together on a die match each other extremely well but their absolute values move roughly ten percent from wafer to wafer, because a few microns' difference anywhere in the stack-up changes how every device on that wafer performs.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can be very well matched, but they won't match on the next wafer that is produced. They might be like 10% off in value
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Integrated design therefore works in ratios rather than absolute values: a divider made from three identically drawn resistors still produces the same output fractions on the next wafer even though every resistor's absolute value has shifted.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do it by designing with ratios. So like you do the ratios between components, not precise values
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Discrete MOSFETs do not carry ESD protection by default. Protection requires a specific suffixed variant, only a small number of parts offer it, and many of those are dual or quad devices intended for logic-level input protection rather than general switching.
claims.quote_verbatim: have to get a specific ESD variant
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Electrical Archeology

claims.claim_text: Once a design has established that it needs the protected variant somewhere, consolidating onto it across the whole board is usually right: the parts differ by a few cents, and mixing two nearly identical devices leaves the reasoning invisible to whoever repairs the board later.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you already decided, okay, I need the ESD part in that part of my circuit because reasons. Then why wouldn't you just like bomb consolidate right across the design
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Electrical Archeology

claims.claim_text: A shorted switch does not only stop the circuit working: one holding a load permanently connected deep-discharged the battery pack to zero volts, destroying cells that could not afterwards be recovered by any slow-charge revival attempt.
claims.quote_verbatim: the MOSFET was shorted, right? So it deep discharged the batteries
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Electrical Archeology

claims.claim_text: Some MOSFETs are export-controlled and cannot be bought outside the United States, because devices fast enough for certain switching applications fall under weapons-related restrictions — a sourcing constraint that has nothing to do with the electrical specification.
claims.quote_verbatim: of the US, you can't even buy certain MOSFETs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rigorous engineering stuff may be out the window

claims.claim_text: An automotive high-side switch is a MOSFET with protection built in — against transients, over-temperature and over-current — and is driven from a plain logic level, so the designer gets the protection behaviour without designing any of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: automotive high side switches are like, you know, a MOSFET, just that it has some added intelligence
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: A vehicle's 12-volt line carries enough transient energy that an ordinary DC-DC converter is likely to fail in service, so the automotive-rated part is a reliability requirement rather than a certification formality.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are a lot of transients on the, like the 12 volt line on a typical car. So there is a high chance that typical converter might fail
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: Package size and safe operating area move together: larger power devices give more margin, and shrinking the package quickly runs the designer out of available parts — which is where intermediate surface-mount packages like the D2PAK, essentially a TO-220 with the tab folded for reflow, exist to fill the gap.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're going with bigger transistors, you get more like safe operating area kind of behavior. But when you start going smaller, you start running out of options
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: A synchronous converter is any conventional topology with the rectifying diode replaced by an actively switched FET, which removes the diode's forward conduction loss — at the cost of needing timing and control that a diode requires none of.
claims.quote_verbatim: those pesky power losing diodes replaced with a switch within intelligent FET
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Here for a reason

claims.claim_text: Converters that must start from nothing keep an ordinary diode for the initial bootstrap and then switch to a synchronous rectifier placed in parallel with it once the internal circuitry has power, taking the efficiency penalty only during start-up.
claims.quote_verbatim: once it starts up and you've got enough voltage to bootstrap it and then power the internal circuitry, then the internal circuitry can then power a synchronous rectifier that's in parallel with the internal diode
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 3D Printed Shark Jumps - Edifying Edison's Energy

claims.claim_text: For a buck converter the two switching devices can be bought as one package with the source of one already tied to the drain of the other and separate high and low gate pins, which simplifies the layout and cuts the losses that the interconnection between two separate parts would add.
claims.quote_verbatim: found this part from TI that has both of them in one package. And so they're connected. The source of one's connected to the drain of the other
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: Trailing-edge dimming needs a bidirectional switch built as two N-channel MOSFETs in inverse series with their sources tied together. Those joined sources are the drive reference and they swing with the mains, so every channel needs its own completely floating gate supply — a problem that multiplies with channel count.
claims.quote_verbatim: you use a pair of back-to-back series MOSFETs as a switching element
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Mains dimmers are hard to protect against short circuits because fault currents rise so fast that the semiconductor fails before the fuse does — the standard dark joke being that the MOSFET blows to protect the fuse.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's rather difficult to short, protect them against short circuits because you get rather high fault currents
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The answer is to detect the fault within the half cycle rather than to fuse it: an isolated Hall-effect sensor in an SO8 with an internal half-milliohm shunt reports plus or minus ten amps as zero to 3.3 volts centred at 1.65 volts, and cutting the drive as the current climbs from the zero crossing saves the device even when switched into a dead short.
claims.quote_verbatim: as soon as it detects an overcurrent during the cycle, it would immediately cut the drive
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Because the sensed current is bipolar around a mid-rail reference, a windowed converter that flags when the signal leaves a band between two limits does in one peripheral what would otherwise need a comparator whose polarity is flipped every half cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got a thresholding ATD converter
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A gate driver is not always required: a microcontroller pin rated for 50 milliamps of drive can switch a MOSFET directly in a low-power high-voltage supply, with one further pin taken back as feedback.
claims.quote_verbatim: MOSFET driver. Forget that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: A high-voltage flyback supply can be built by treating one winding of a small step-up transformer as a plain inductor: clamp it to ground while the other side charges from the low-voltage rail, release it, and the secondary presents ten times the flyback voltage into a diode and capacitor.
claims.quote_verbatim: you use one leg of the transformer and pretend it's an inductor. So you like clamp it to ground
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: When a module's own low-power modes will not meet the current budget its datasheet implies, cutting its supply entirely with a low-side N-channel switch is the reliable fallback, and the firmware then has to take on measuring the available energy and adapting its measurement and upload rates to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: just stuck a low side end channel MOSFET in there just to shut the power off to the whole modem
claims.speaker: Ray Ozzie
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ray Ozzie (Blues Wireless)

claims.claim_text: Supply glitching for fault injection needs no more than a MOSFET used as a crowbar for a few nanoseconds: it drains the bypass capacitance, the rail droops while the capacitor recharges, and that droop is the attack.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has is like a MOSFET basically. So it's doing a, you know, a crowbar type thing, just very short, like, you know, nanoseconds
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: The simplest possible backscatter retroreflector is a MOSFET with an antenna on it, shorting the antenna under gate control; more elaborate modulation at the reflector is possible but the minimal version needs no more parts than that.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically just a MOSFET, you know, a MOSFET with an antenna attached
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Driving anything outside the board from a single-board computer should go through a FET on a separate power domain, so a fault destroys the transistor or blows the domain's fuse rather than the processor — the difference between a cheap part and a replaced board.
claims.quote_verbatim: put a FET between your Broadcom or whatever it is your Raspberry Pi in the world and then put it on a separate power domain
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: Switching resistors in and out with MOSFETs under plain digital control is enough to make a regulator's set point or a load's current programmable, with no analog output anywhere in the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have MOSFETs that we're just turning on and off directly from the Raspberry Pi Pico
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Where a low-impedance path has to hold its value against time and temperature, a MOSFET is a poor substitute for a relay: on-resistance moves with temperature, and the device's own dissipation heats it, so there is no guaranteed constant value without adding thermal control around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: low impedance path. And I need it not to vary with time or temperature
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: The trade runs the other way on lifetime: a relay is a physical mechanism with a rated life that changes as it wears, while a semiconductor switch kept inside its thermal ratings has no wear mechanism and can be operated indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: solid state semiconductor can, you know, be used an infinite amount of times in theory
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: At a build quantity of ten, selecting the switching device and inductor, running the calculations and then debugging oscillation costs more than an off-the-shelf converter module — the design effort only pays back at volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're only making a small run of, you know, 10 or something, you just buy a off the shelf power brick
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Robo Fry Guy

claims.claim_text: A single shared dropper resistor for a multi-segment display makes brightness depend on how many segments are lit, because the available current is shared among whatever is on — visible as digits that dim as more of them illuminate.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you turn on all the segments, then, you know, you're going to get like the, the current, the maximum amount of current has to be shared
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: A design can dispense with dropper resistors entirely by relying on the on-resistance of a logic chip's high-side output devices, and that effective output resistance is derivable from the datasheet's output-high voltage drop at a stated output current.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're relying on the RDS on of the output MOSFET, the high side output MOSFETs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: Totem-pole CMOS outputs can degrade asymmetrically: when the upper device weakens the pin can no longer pull high, and because a totem pole has no pull-up resistor the failure is total. Adding an external pull-up recovers it, but at 25 MHz into a capacitive bus that means a hundred ohms and tens of milliamps.
claims.quote_verbatim: the upper transistor might've failed. So it can't pull up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shine A Light

claims.claim_text: Logic inputs carry a maximum input slew rate — on the order of 500 nanoseconds for common HC-family parts — and a signal slower than that voids the guarantee: the input can enter a metastable state, and a clock line doing so will oscillate unpredictably rather than simply run slow.
claims.quote_verbatim: if the slew rate of your input signal is too slow
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shine A Light

claims.claim_text: Slowing an edge cuts the impulse current delivered into the trace capacitance and so lowers average power, but the same slow edge burns power in a MOSFET crossing its transition region and can push non-Schmitt logic inputs into instability — the optimum is a balance rather than a direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: slower you make your, um, your transition, the less impulse current goes into your capacitive trace
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: World Trade Futurity (WTF)

claims.claim_text: MOSFETs are the easier device to fabricate outside a fab: a bipolar needs a very accurate furnace because the emitter and collector diffusions must meet the base without overrunning it, a process controlled by temperature and time together, whereas a MOSFET needs an oxide grown to a thickness you can judge by its colour.
claims.quote_verbatim: bipolars are a little bit more difficult at home because you need a furnace that's very accurate
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: FinFET names a shape rather than a new device: as gate lengths shrink, the geometry goes vertical to recover gate surface area within the same footprint on the die.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to get more surface area on a gate, what you do is you start using weird-ass geometries
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: A CMOS inverter is two complementary MOSFETs in a totem pole with their gates tied together as the input and their outputs tied together — the signal drives both gates at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: a CMOS inverter is simply two gates
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: Teaching bipolars first is a defensible tradition but a poor fit for practice: they are harder to reason about because the behaviour is neither purely current-controlled nor purely voltage-controlled, and the device most people actually use is the FET — so the FET is the better starting point with bipolars later.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the transistors you actually end up using day to day today are probably going to be MOSFETs
claims.speaker: Michal Zalewski
claims.episode_title: The Secret Life of Circuits with lcamtuf / Michał Zalewski

claims.claim_text: A single-electron readout is a deliberately non-linear MOSFET around 50 by 100 nanometres: at nanometre distances, moving one electron nearby shifts the bias point by the equivalent of some tens of millivolts, which is enough to switch the device from off to on when the whole system is held near absolute zero.
claims.quote_verbatim: the readout device is actually essentially a modified MOSFET
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello
claims.episode_title: Quantum Computing with Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: In an electric drivetrain the loss budget is dominated by conduction drops at every element: the inverter's switch drops account for about two percent at full power and the battery's internal impedance about three percent, which is why low impedance everywhere is a system-level requirement rather than a component preference.
claims.quote_verbatim: out the inverter is a 2% loss under full power. The batteries are in that area, maybe 3
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Comparative part selection work — buying a spread of candidate devices, testing them against each other, plotting the results and writing it up — happens constantly inside companies and essentially never gets published, so the same characterisation is repeated privately many times over.
claims.quote_verbatim: okay, we need to choose the best 500-volt MOSFET
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: EcoWoke and Going Broke

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep196 (Mike Engelhardt) and ep719 (Alex Lidow) both label some host questions with the guest's name; claims were assigned by content, and only material clearly belonging to the guest was kept.
ep539 (Big Clive), ep568 (Florin of Voltlog), ep498 (Andrea Morello) and ep640 carry the same single-speaker pattern; only unambiguous guest material was used.
ep589 alternates between the two hosts cleanly enough to attribute by content: the simulator beta discovery is Chris Gammell's, the bipolar-versus-field-effect distinction is Dave Jones's.
One passage in the bundle carries episode: null and was dropped as uncitable.
The Miller plateau description in ep500 is explicitly hedged by the speaker; the claim keeps only the part he states plainly.
